testCases.input: Examine the constitutional safeguards against executive abuse of the ordinance-making power. How did the Supreme Court curb mechanical re-promulgation in D.C. Wadhwa and Krishna Kumar Singh?
testCases.actualOutput: Under Article 123 (for the President) and Article 213 (for the Governor), an ordinance can only be promulgated when both or either House of Parliament/State Legislature is not in session and circumstances exist which render it necessary to take immediate action. The Constitution mandates that an ordinance must be laid before the legislature and ceases to operate after six weeks from the reassembly of the legislature. In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court held that the mechanical and repeated re-promulgation of ordinances without placing them before the legislative assembly is a subversion of the democratic legislative process, a colorable exercise of power, and a fraud on the Constitution. In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), a 7-judge Constitution bench reaffirmed that ordinance-making is an exceptional emergency power, that tabling the ordinance before the legislature is mandatory, and that the executive's satisfaction is not immune from judicial review.

## 4. Subsequent Re-affirmation in *Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar* (2017)
In 2017, a 7-judge Constitution Bench in *Krishna Kumar Singh* re-examined and fortified *D.C. Wadhwa*, holding that:
- Placing an ordinance before the legislature is a mandatory constitutional requirement.
- Re-promulgation is unconstitutional per se.
- The satisfaction of the President/Governor under Articles 123 and 213 is subject to judicial review.

---

## 5. UPSC Mains Exam Application
- **Polity GS2 Hook**: The primary legal benchmark for questions on "Ordinance Making Powers of President and Governor (Art 123/213)", "Decline of Parliamentary Scrutiny", and "Separation of Powers".

## 3. Majority Ratio Decidendi (Unanimous 5-0 Ruling, Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati)
1. **Re-promulgation is a Fraud on the Constitution**:
   The Supreme Court struck down the practice of re-promulgating ordinances as **unconstitutional, a colorable exercise of power, and a subversion of the democratic legislative process**.
   > *"The executive cannot usurp the legislative function of the legislature by repeatedly re-promulgating ordinances without submitting them to the assembly. Such an exercise of power is a subversion of the democratic process and a fraud on the Constitution."*

2. **Emergency Exception vs Normal Rule**:
   The power to make ordinances under Article 123 and Article 213 is an **extraordinary emergency power** granted to the executive to deal with urgent, unforeseen situations when the legislature is not in session. It cannot be converted into an everyday substitute for the primary law-making power of the elected legislature.

[D C Wadhwa 1987]
---

## 1. Background & Core Facts
Dr. D.C. Wadhwa, a professor of economics at the Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics in Pune, conducted thorough empirical research into the legislative practices of the State of Bihar. He discovered an astonishing constitutional subversion: between 1967 and 1981, the Governor of Bihar promulgated **256 ordinances**, and all of them were kept alive for years (some for over 14 years!) through repeated re-promulgation on the exact same terms immediately after the prorogation of each legislative session, without ever placing the bills before the State Legislature. Dr. Wadhwa filed a public interest writ petition under Article 32 challenging this systemic "Ordinance Raj".

---

[D C Wadhwa 1987]
3. **Mandatory Legislative Scrutiny**:
   An ordinance must be laid before the Legislative Assembly as soon as it reconvenes and will cease to operate at the expiration of 6 weeks from reassembly. Allowing the executive to bypass the legislature and govern purely by decree destroys the core principle of constitutional separation of powers.

4. **Locus Standi Recognized**:
   The Court recognized that every citizen has a vital interest in ensuring that the governance of the state is conducted according to the Constitution and rule of law, affirming Dr. Wadhwa's PIL standing.

[Article 123 - Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament]
Article 123 - Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament

(1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.

 

(2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance —

 

(a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and

 

(b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President.

 

      Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.

 

(3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void.

[Puttaswamy 2017]

## 2. Key Constitutional Questions
1. Does the Indian Constitution guarantee a fundamental Right to Privacy?
2. If so, which provision of the Constitution protects it?

1. **Privacy is an Inalienable Fundamental Right**:
   The Court unanimously held that the **Right to Privacy is a fundamental right**, protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under **Article 21** and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

2. **Overruled Precedents**:
   The Court explicitly overruled *M.P. Sharma* (1954) and *Kharak Singh* (1962) to the extent that they held privacy was not a fundamental right.

## 1. Background & Core Facts
Minerva Mills, a textile undertaking in Bangalore, was nationalized by the Central Government under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1974. The owners challenged the takeover and simultaneously challenged the constitutional validity of Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (enacted during the Emergency). 
- Section 55 had inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368, claiming that amendments made by Parliament could never be questioned in any court and stating there was no limitation whatever on Parliament's amending power.
- Section 4 had expanded Article 31C to give blanket precedence to **all** Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) over Fundamental Rights under Articles 14 and 19.

1. **Invalidation of Article 368(4) and (5) (Unlimited Amending Power Struck Down)**:
   The Court held that **a limited amending power is itself a basic feature of the Constitution**. Parliament cannot, by exercising its limited power under Article 368, enlarge that very power into an absolute or unlimited power. Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 were declared unconstitutional because they abolished judicial review and destroyed the Basic Structure.

[Kesavananda 1973]

## 3. Majority Ratio Decidendi (7-6 Majority)

   The Supreme Court overruled *Golaknath* and held that Parliament has the power to amend any and every part of the Constitution, including Part III (Fundamental Rights). However, this amending power under Article 368 is not unlimited: **it does not extend to damaging, destroying, or altering the "Basic Structure" or essential identity of the Constitution.**
   
2. **Constituent Power vs Total Destruction**:
   Justice H.R. Khanna delivered the pivotal concurring judgment, observing that the word "amendment" postulates that the old Constitution survives without loss of its identity despite changes in details. Parliament cannot use Article 368 to replace the Constitution with a completely different framework or create a sovereign legislature in place of constitutional supremacy.

[Maneka Gandhi 1978]

testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: How did the landmark S.R. Bommai judgment provide safeguards against the partisan invocation of Article 356 (President's Rule)?
testCases.actualOutput: Article 356 empowers the President to impose President's Rule in a State upon receiving a report from the Governor or otherwise if satisfied that the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a 9-judge Constitution bench held that federalism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. The Court laid down that presidential proclamations under Article 356 are subject to judicial review, and the executive's satisfaction must be based on objective, relevant material. The Court mandated that the floor of the Legislative Assembly is the only constitutional forum to test a Ministry's majority (Floor Test). Crucially, Bommai ruled that the Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved until both Houses of Parliament approve the proclamation, and the Court has the power to restore a dismissed government and revive a dissolved assembly if the proclamation is found to be malafide or unconstitutional.

# S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)

- **Citation**: (1994) 3 SCC 1; AIR 1994 SC 1918
- **Decided On**: March 11, 1994
- **Bench Strength**: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
- **Bench Members**: S.R. Pandian, A.M. Ahmadi, Kuldip Singh, J.S. Verma, P.B. Sawant, K. Ramaswamy, S.C. Agrawal, Yogeshwar Dayal, and B.P. Jeevan Reddy JJ.
- **Constitutional Provisions Interpreted**: Article 356, Article 355, Article 74(2), Article 163, Basic Structure Doctrine

---

## 1. Background & Core Facts
In 1989, the Janata Dal government led by S.R. Bommai in Karnataka was dismissed by the Governor following defections, without giving the Chief Minister an opportunity to prove his majority on the floor of the Legislative Assembly. Simultaneously, following the demolition of the Babri Masjid in December 1992, the President dismissed BJP-led state governments in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Himachal Pradesh on grounds of threats to secularism and public order.

---

[Sr Bommai 1994]
2. **Judicial Review of Article 356**:
   A proclamation under Article 356 is **not immune from judicial review**. The courts can examine whether the material on which the President formed satisfaction was relevant, whether there was malafide intent, or whether the exercise of power was based on extraneous considerations.

3. **Floor Test is Mandatory**:
   The floor of the Legislative Assembly is the **only legitimate constitutional forum** to test whether a government commands a majority. A Governor’s subjective assessment or "headcount" at Raj Bhavan is impermissible.

[Sr Bommai 1994]
---

## 2. Key Constitutional Questions
1. Is the presidential proclamation imposing President's Rule under Article 356 subject to judicial review?
2. What is the scope of "satisfaction of the President" under Article 356(1)?
3. Does Article 74(2) bar courts from examining the material basis on which the Council of Ministers advised the President?
4. Are Federalism and Secularism part of the Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution?
5. Where should a Chief Minister's majority be tested—in Raj Bhavan or on the floor of the Assembly?

---

## 3. Majority Ratio Decidendi
1. **Federalism and Secularism are Basic Structure Pillars**:
   The 9-judge bench authoritatively held that both **Federalism** and **Secularism** are essential and inviolable features of the Basic Structure. Any state government acting against secularism can be subjected to action under Article 356.

[Sr Bommai 1994]
4. **Remedy of Restoration & Status Quo Ante**:
   - The Legislative Assembly should not be dissolved immediately upon issuing an Article 356 proclamation; it can only be suspended. Dissolution is permitted only after both Houses of Parliament approve the proclamation.
   - If the proclamation is struck down by the courts as unconstitutional, the court has the power to restore the dismissed government and revive the dissolved assembly.

---

## 4. Operative Guidelines for Governors and Union Executive
- Warning requirement: The Centre must issue a warning notice under Article 355 before invoking Article 356, except in extraordinary emergencies.
- Floor test must be ordered within the shortest possible timeframe (typically 48 hours).
- Article 356 is an exceptional power and should be treated as a measure of "last resort".

---

[Article 357 - Exercise of legislative powers under Proclamation issued under article 356]
Article 357 - Exercise of legislative powers under Proclamation issued under article 356

(1) Where by a Proclamation issued under clause (1) of article 356, it has been declared that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, it shall be competent —

 

(a) for Parliament to confer on the President the power of the Legislature of the State to make laws, and to authorise the President to delegate, subject to such conditions as he may think fit to impose, the power so conferred to any other authority to be specified by him in that behalf;

 

(b) for Parliament, or for the President or other authority in whom such power to make laws is vested under sub-clause (a), to make laws conferring powers and imposing duties, or authorising the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the Union or officers and authorities thereof;

 

(c) for the President to authorise when the House of the People is not in session expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State pending the sanction of such expenditure by Parliament.

 

(2) Any law made in exercise of the power of the Legislature of the State by Parliament or the President or other authority referred to in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) which Parliament or the President or such other authority would not, but for the issue of a Proclamation under article 356, have been competent to make shall, after the Proclamation has ceased to operate, continue in force until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other authority.

[Kesavananda 1973]

While not exhaustively defined, the judges identified key illustrative pillars:
- Supremacy of the Constitution
- Republican and Democratic form of Government
- Secular character of the Constitution
- Separation of powers between the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary
- Federal character of the Constitution
- Sovereignty and integrity of India
- Fundamental Rights and Dignity of the Individual
- Power of Judicial Review

- **Exam Hook**: Acts as an indestructible safety valve preserving constitutionalism against parliamentary majoritarianism and executive authoritarianism.

4. **Timing of Judicial Intervention (No Quo Warranto at Interlocutory Stage)**:
   Judicial review cannot be invoked at an interlocutory stage prior to the Speaker making an order. The courts will not interfere while the proceedings are pending before the Speaker, but will exercise review once a final decision is rendered.

---

## 4. Key Dissenting Opinion (Minority - J.S. Verma and L.M. Sharma JJ.)
The minority held that the Speaker is an active partisan member of a political party and dependent on the ruling party's continuous support; therefore, vesting exclusive and final adjudicatory power in the Speaker violates the Basic Structure of democracy. They recommended an independent tribunal or the Election Commission.

[Article 356 - Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States]
Article 356 - Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States

(1) If the President, on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution, the President may by Proclamation —

 

(a) assume to himself all or any of the functions of the Government of the State and all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor or any body or authority in the State other than the Legislature of the State;

 

(b) declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament;

 

(c) make such incidental and consequential provisions as appear to the President to be necessary or desirable for giving effect to the objects of the Proclamation, including provisions for suspending in whole or in part the operation of any provisions of this Constitution relating to any body or authority in the State:

 

   Provided that nothing in this clause shall authorise the President to assume to himself any of the powers vested in or exercisable by a High Court, or to suspend in whole or in part the operation of any provision of this Constitution relating to High Courts.

 

(2) Any such Proclamation may be revoked or varied by a subsequent Proclamation.

 

(3) Every Proclamation under this article shall be laid before each House of Parliament and shall, except where it is a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation, cease to operate at the expiration of two months unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament:

 

   Provided that if any such Proclamation (not being a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation) is issued at a time when the House of the People is dissolved or the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during the period of two months referred to in this clause, and if a resolution approving the Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People before the expiration of that period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days a resolution approving the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People.

 

(4) A Proclamation so approved shall, unless revoked, cease to operate on the expiration of a period of six months from the date of issue of the Proclamation:

 

   Provided that if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force of such a Proclamation is passed by both Houses of Parliament, the Proclamation shall, unless revoked, continue in force for a further period of six months from the date on which under this clause it would otherwise have ceased to operate, but no such Proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than three years:

 

   Provided further that if the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during any such period of six months and a resolution approving the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People during the said period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days a resolution approving the continuance in force of the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People:

 

   Provided also that in the case of the Proclamation issued under clause (1) on the 11th day of May, 1987 with respect to the State of Punjab, the reference in the first proviso to this clause to “three years” shall be construed as a reference to five years.

 

(5) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (4), a resolution with respect to the continuance in force of a Proclamation approved under clause (3) for any period beyond the expiration of one year from the date of issue of such Proclamation shall not be passed by either House of Parliament unless —

 

(a) a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, in the whole of India or, as the case may be, in the whole or any part of the State, at the time of the passing of such resolution, and

 

(b) the Election Commission certifies that the continuance in force of the Proclamation approved under clause (3) during the period specified in such resolution is necessary on account of difficulties in holding general elections to the Legislative Assembly of the State concerned:

 

   Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to the Proclamation issued under clause (1) on the 11th day of May, 1987 with respect to the State of Punjab.

testCases.input: How did the Supreme Court's ruling in Lily Thomas v. Union of India transform the disqualification regime for convicted lawmakers under the RPA 1951?
testCases.actualOutput: Under Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act (RPA), 1951, lawmakers face disqualification upon conviction for criminal offences. While Section 8(1) and 8(2) specify particular offences, Section 8(3) lays down that a person convicted of any offence and sentenced to imprisonment for not less than two years stands disqualified from the date of conviction and for a further six years post-release. Previously, Section 8(4) carved out a protective window for sitting MPs and MLAs, stating that disqualification would not take effect for three months or until an appeal/revision was disposed of by a court. In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) as ultra vires Articles 102(1)(e) and 191(1)(e) of the Constitution, holding that Parliament lacked the legislative competence to create a distinction between candidates seeking election and sitting legislators, making disqualification instantaneous upon sentencing.
